At the door, on Horea Street

Nora Lindqvist, an architect from Sweden, has just arrived in Cluj-Napoca. She will spend a year restoring old buildings. She has rented a room in a flat on Horea Street and is ringing her landlady’s doorbell.
Good evening! Excuse me, are you Mrs Pop?
Yes, that’s me. Good evening! And you are…?
My name is Nora Lindqvist. I’m the new tenant.
Ah, Nora! Pleased to meet you! I’m Elisabeta Pop. You’re not Romanian, are you?
No, I’m not Romanian. I’m Swedish.
Swedish! And where are you from?
I’m from Gothenburg. It’s a big city by the sea.
Lovely! I’m from Cluj, from here. Are you a student?
No, I’m an architect. I’m working on a project here, in the centre.
Very good! Welcome to Cluj! Here are the keys.
Thank you very much, Mrs Pop!
You’re welcome. And this is Mițu, my tomcat. Good night, Nora! See you tomorrow!

to be: eu sunt (I am) / ei sunt (they are)
pleased to meet you (said by a woman)
a, an (indefinite article, masculine and neuter)
here you are (please take it, formal)
A short, neutral sound with a relaxed mouth, like the “a” in English “about” or the “e” in French “le”. It is unstressed.
The same sound written in two ways. It is pronounced in the middle of the mouth, with lips spread, like an “i” said from the throat. Write “î” at the beginning and end of a word, “â” inside it.
“ce” and “ci” are read like “che”, “chi” in English “check”, “chin” (as in Italian “ciao”). “che” and “chi” are read with a “k”: “chei” = “kay”.
“ge” and “gi” are read like English “j” (“jeans”). “ghe” and “ghi” are read with a hard “g”: “ghid”.
Romanians greet a lot, and the greeting changes with the time of day and with how well you know the person.
from 11 until evening; the safest greeting
only at bedtime or when leaving late at night
any time, with friends and young people
“Bună!” on its own is very common among friends, even in the morning or evening.
Romanian has a polite form: “dumneavoastră”. The verb is in the second person plural, as with “voi” (you, plural). “Tu” is used with friends, family, children and young colleagues.
a stranger, an adult, a boss
a friend, a child, a young colleague
When talking about a lady or a gentleman you say “doamna Pop” (Mrs Pop) and “domnul Pop” (Mr Pop). When addressing someone directly you will also hear “doamnă!”, “domnule!”.
With someone older, always start with “dumneavoastră”. Switch to “tu” only when the person suggests it.
2nd person plural; also the polite form

The pronoun can be dropped, because the verb form already shows the person: “Sunt Nora” is more natural than “Eu sunt Nora”. Keep the pronoun when you want to stress it: “Eu sunt din Cluj, nu el.” (I am from Cluj, not him.)
“Este” is very often shortened to “e”: “Mițu e motanul meu.” (Mițu is my tomcat.)
As in Spanish or Italian, jobs are said without an article: “Sunt arhitectă” (I am an architect), not “Sunt o arhitectă”.
The feminine form is often made with -ă (student → studentă) or with -oaică (englez → englezoaică).
Nationalities and languages are written with a small letter: “sunt suedeză”, “vorbesc română”.
Negation is simple: “nu” goes before the verb.
Mrs Pop is not a student.
In yes/no questions the word order stays the same. Only the intonation changes: the voice rises at the end.
“…, nu?” at the end asks for confirmation: “Nu sunteți româncă, nu?” (You’re not Romanian, are you?)
Romanian uses the Latin alphabet and has five special letters: ă, â, î, ș, ț. They are called diacritics and they change the meaning of words.
In the app you can type without diacritics: the answer is accepted, but we show you the correct form. Still, try to use them from the start, with the buttons under the input field.
“ș” and “ț” are written with a comma below, not a cedilla (ş, ţ). Some old keyboards produce the cedilla; the app accepts both.
